content:
Sam Shamoun has written against Islam for more than twenty-five years. He was one of the most prolific writers on Answering Islam, the site run by Jochen Katz, and he now debates and broadcasts online, funded by his followers. Even a friendly Christian news site, profiling him in 2024, headlined him an "unhinged, fiery Assyrian evangelist" and opened with the words "Pugnacious debater Sam Shamoun".[1]

Most of what he publishes asks the reader to take his word: that a hadith says what he says it says, that a classical scholar meant what he claims, that a Muslim opponent has been refuted. So a prior question deserves an answer. How does his own word hold up when it is tested under oath?

This article aims to provide context to that question, insha'Allah, in seven findings from the two opinions the Appellate Court of Illinois published in 2020 in his divorce case.[2] Everything is quoted as the court wrote it. The personal matters of his former wife and their two children are theirs, and we leave them aside.

He told the court that he was "employed as a Christian apologist and Bible teacher", but when he was asked what he earned, he "could not remember" his income "for 2016, 2017, or 2018 year to date".

The trial judge, who heard him over a two-day trial, found that his testimony "was inconsistent, contradicted by other evidence, and not credible". The appellate court, which defers to the judge who sees the witness, let that finding stand.[3]

Strength: firm. It is a finding of the trial court, upheld on appeal, about the man who asks his audience to trust his reading of sources.

His W-2 forms show $116,500 for 2016 (he testified, and the court accepted, that the true figure was $100,000) and $50,081 for 2017, the year the divorce was filed. The trial court called the drop one "without explanation".

He told the court that donors had fallen away. The appellate court could not weigh that testimony, because no transcript of the trial was in the record.[4]

Strength: moderate. The figures are in the record and the trial court rejected his account of them; the reason he gave was never tested on appeal.

He conceded that he "regularly receives gifts and donations" that did not appear on his tax forms, and said that he "does not consider [those sums] to be income". Donations were also paid into his Patreon accounts, he said, yet he "provided no documents" for them and could not recall the amounts.

From a single checking account the court traced a further $15,078.24 received in 2017. It concluded that he had "additional income available to him other than what [he] disclosed", and named "[the] fact that Sam receives additional income which he has not disclosed" among its reasons for the child-support order.[5]

Strength: firm. Those who fund his work against Islam may reflect that a court could not establish how much they had given him, because he did not disclose it.

Ordered to pay temporary support, he failed to comply, and fees were assessed against him for the cost of enforcing the order. He failed to comply again, neither responded nor appeared at the hearing, and paid only after the deadline was extended.

When a further fee award went unpaid, the court issued and stayed a body attachment, an order for his arrest, to compel payment. The record does not show whether he then paid.[6]

Strength: firm. The orders, the missed deadlines and the body attachment are set out in the opinion.

The trial court granted a motion against him because of his "deficient production of documents" and his failure "to provide updated discovery", and barred him from offering evidence he had not disclosed.

When his wife petitioned for her fees after the trial, he did not respond to the petition, and neither he nor his lawyer came to the hearing.[7] Strength: firm. A man who asks others to show their sources did not show his own to a court that ordered him to.

In November 2017, at his wife's request, the court entered a two-year order prohibiting him from "harassing, stalking, or physically abusing" her, granting her sole possession of the marital home and barring him from the home and her place of work.[8]

In its final judgment the court found that he had "needlessly increased the cost of [the] litigation", among other ways "by engaging in conduct that necessitated the entry of an order of protection against him".[9]

Strength: firm on the order and the finding. The opinions do not describe the conduct, and we do not go beyond what they say.

In August 2019 the circuit court had his financial affidavit and his bank statements before it. When he pleaded that he could not afford his wife's fees for the appeal, it called the claim "totally disingenuous".

It found that he "[had] not been paying the maintenance and child support despite having the funds available" to do so.[10] Strength: firm. His second appeal, against that fee order, was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

The bottom line

The appellate court upheld the maintenance award and the award of fees, and let the findings on his income and credibility stand.[11]

A man's private failures are not, by themselves, an argument against what he writes, and Muslims are commanded to judge fairly even those they oppose: "let not the hatred of others to you make you swerve to wrong and depart from justice."[12] We cite this record because his method is to set himself up as a judge of character: he calls the Prophet (peace be upon him) a liar and a false prophet, and asks his audience to trust his reading of sources they cannot check.

When his own statements were tested under oath, by a judge with the documents in front of her, they were found inconsistent, contradicted by the evidence and not credible. His own scripture sets the standard: "if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever."[13]

Readers who meet his claims about Islam should weigh them as the Illinois courts weighed his testimony: against the documents. Our replies on the subjects he writes about include the Islamic dilemma, makr and the charge that God deceives, the Satanic Verses report, the questions about Aisha and where Jesus said he is God. God knows best.

Notes

  1. Michael Ashcraft, "Unhinged, fiery Assyrian evangelist got his start at six", God Reports, 23 August 2024.

App. Ct. August 20, 2020). The respondent is named in both as Hassamo (Sam) Shamoun.
  3. 2020 IL App (1st) 182710, paragraphs 15 and 42.
  4. Ibid., paragraphs 15, 16 and 43.
  5. Ibid., paragraphs 16, 17 and 20.
  6. Ibid., paragraphs 7 to 9.
  7. Ibid., paragraphs 11 and 12.
  8. Ibid., paragraph 5.
  9. Ibid., paragraphs 22 and 70.
  10. No. 1-19-1840, 159 N.E.3d 538, paragraphs 7 and 17 to 20.
  11. 2020 IL App (1st) 182710, paragraph 76.

  13. 1 Timothy 5:8, ESV.
